sentences.text: This is part one of Differentiation.

The lecturer calls Chapter four of the notes a review of A-level maths.
So these videos rebuild it from the foundations.
And they slow down on the parts people only half remember: implicit differentiation, Leibniz's formula, and classifying stationary points.
Everything in this lecture is about functions of one variable.
Taking a function of two variables and differentiating it in different directions is called partial differentiation.
That comes in Chapter seven of the notes, and next term.
So start at the very beginning: a curve, and a line through two of its points.
Slide one point towards the other, and the line swings round until it just touches the curve.
What exactly is a derivative?
And when does it fail to exist?
Take a function of one variable, why of ex, drawn in blue.
Pick a point on it, at ex.
Now step along by a small amount, delta ex, to a second point, at ex plus delta ex.
Between the two points, the curve rises by delta why: the height at the second point, minus the height at the first.
The line through the two points is called the chord.
Its slope is the rise over the run, delta why over delta ex.
Here's an example: why equals ex cubed, at ex equals one.
With delta ex equal to a half, the chord's slope is four point seven five.
With a tenth, it's three point three one.
With a hundredth, three point zero three.
As delta ex shrinks, the chords swing round and settle on one line, the tangent line.
Here its slope is three.
That slope is the derivative, the gradient of the curve at that point.
So here's the definition.
The derivative of why with respect to ex is the limit, as delta ex goes to zero, of delta why over delta ex.
Chapter five of the notes does limits properly.
For now, closer and closer is enough.
Look closely at that limit.
The top goes to zero, and so does the bottom.
Newton's idea, in effect, divides zero by zero, and in the seventeenth century that was controversial.
Yet the ratio heads somewhere definite, here to three.
As the lecturer puts it, another mathematical crisis successfully resolved.
One property follows straight away: differentiation is a linear operation.
The derivative of a sum is the sum of the derivatives, and a constant factor comes out in front.
That's because the quotient for a sum splits into one quotient per function, and limits add up the same way.
So why do those chord slopes head for three?
Work it out from first principles.
The lecturer's recipe has five steps: substitute, expand, subtract, divide, and take the limit.
First, substitute ex plus delta ex into ex cubed.
Expand the cube.
You get ex cubed, plus three ex squared times delta ex, plus three ex times delta ex squared, plus delta ex cubed.
Now subtract why of ex, which is ex cubed.
It cancels the first term.
Every term that's left has at least one factor of delta ex.
Divide by delta ex.
Each term loses one factor of it.
You get three ex squared, plus three ex times delta ex, plus delta ex squared.
At ex equals one, with delta ex equal to a half, this comes to four point seven five.
That's the first chord slope you saw.
Now let delta ex go to zero.
The last two terms each carry a factor of delta ex, so they go to zero.
What's left is three ex squared.
That's the power rule you already know: the power comes down in front, and the new power is one less.
At ex equals one, it gives three, the slope of the tangent line.
The notes add a condition here: if delta ex is smaller than one in size, each power of it is smaller than the last.
The lecturer says you can skip it: every leftover term has a factor of delta ex, so it goes to zero anyway.
Keep the result on a card, ex cubed to three ex squared.
Part four takes it further.
The symbol in that box, dee why by dee ex, has a history.
Calculus was invented by two people at around the same time, Isaac Newton and Gottfried Leibniz.
Leibniz published in sixteen eighty-six, and Newton in sixteen eighty-seven.
But it seems Newton made his breakthrough some twenty years earlier, in sixteen sixty-five and sixty-six.
Each claimed to be first, and they fell out badly.
Newton's approach was based on limits.
Leibniz used geometric arguments, and a much simpler notation, including dee by dee ex and the integral sign.
Britain kept Newton's notation through the eighteenth century, and the rest of the world, using Leibniz's, made more progress.
Newton's dot, for a derivative with respect to time, survives.
Oiler wrote a capital D, and his student Lagrange gave us primes.

So when part three flips it over, it proves that the flip is allowed.
Now, when does it fail?
Functions are not always differentiable.
Here's an example: why equals mod ex, the absolute value of ex.
To the left of zero it's minus ex, a straight line with slope minus one.
To the right it's just ex, with slope plus one.
And it's continuous.
You can draw it without lifting the pen.
But look at the corner, at zero.
Which line is the tangent line there?
Lots of lines touch the corner, and none of them is the right one.
Chords from the right all have slope plus one.
Chords from the left all have slope minus one.
There's no single slope, so the derivative of mod ex does not exist at zero.
Everywhere else, it's fine.
The second example is the Heaviside step function.
It's zero for negative ex, and one for positive ex.
At zero itself, definitions vary, and the notes leave it out.
The lecturer puts that point in the top piece: a filled dot at height one, and an open circle at the origin.
That way the function has exactly one value at zero.
Away from zero, the graph is flat, so its derivative is zero.
At zero, it's undefined.
To see why, take a chord from the left that crosses the jump.

With delta ex equal to a tenth, that's ten.
With a hundredth, a hundred.
The slope grows without bound, so no tangent line can match it.
So what exactly does differentiable demand?
Here's the lecturer's definition.
F is differentiable at ex if this limit exists, and is finite.
It's the quotient from before: the change in F, over a small step.
She calls the step H, instead of delta ex.
As she says, H is just a variable.
The notes' box says what that takes.
First, the function must be continuous.
Second, the derivative must be finite and defined.
That means the left-hand limit, where you step back from ex by H, must equal the right-hand limit, where you step forward.
Run mod ex through the box, at zero.
It's continuous, so the first test passes.
But the left-hand limit is minus one, and the right-hand limit is plus one.
They disagree, so the second test fails.
Now the Heaviside step function.
Both pieces are flat, with slope zero, so the two sides seem to agree.
But the function jumps, so it is not continuous, and the first test fails.
Indeed, the left-hand quotient is one over the step, which blows up.

If the derivative exists, the change in F is the step, times the difference quotient, which stays finite, so it goes to zero with the step.
So a differentiable function is continuous.
The reverse is false, and mod ex shows it.
Finite matters too.
Where the tangent line is vertical, its slope is infinite.

Time for a recap.
The derivative is the limit of chord slopes, as delta ex goes to zero.
From first principles, you substitute, expand, subtract, divide, and take the limit.
For ex cubed, that gives three ex squared.
At a corner or a jump, there's no derivative.
To be differentiable, a function must be continuous, its left-hand and right-hand limits must agree, and its slope must be finite.
